title: Applied Machine Learning with TensorFlow
subtitle: Build end-to-end TensorFlow projects: tf.data pipelines and preprocessing layers, CNNs and transfer learning for images, TF-IDF and LSTM models for text, and models saved, exported and served.
outcomes: Manage and preprocess tabular, image and text data with tf.data pipelines and Keras preprocessing layers
Construct and train convolutional neural networks for image classification, with data augmentation
Apply transfer learning and fine-tuning to pre-trained models such as MobileNetV2
Develop TF-IDF, embedding and recurrent (LSTM and GRU) models for text analysis and sentiment prediction
Evaluate models with suitable metrics and validation strategies, then save, export and serve them
prerequisites: Introduction to Neural Networks and TensorFlow, or equivalent: tensors, Dense layers, and compiling and fitting Keras models. Python with pandas, plus train/test splits and metrics (Machine Learning Foundations with Python). Install Python 3.10 or later, then pip install tensorflow pandas scikit-learn pillow (TensorFlow 2.16 or later). Module 3 downloads MobileNetV2's weights, about 9 MB, once.
description:
Knowing how a neural network learns is one thing; getting real data into one, choosing the right architecture and shipping the result is another. This course is about the second. You'll build TensorFlow projects end to end on tabular data, images and text: input pipelines with tf.data, preprocessing layers that travel inside the model, and the Keras functional API for models with several inputs. For images you'll build convolutional networks from scratch, then reuse MobileNetV2's ImageNet features through transfer learning and fine-tuning, and meet the ideas behind object detection and segmentation, from IoU to non-maximum suppression.

For text you'll tokenise reviews, weigh up stop words, and compare bag-of-words and TF-IDF classifiers with embeddings and recurrent networks (SimpleRNN, GRU and LSTM), then save, export and serve the model so that it takes raw text. Every lab runs on a laptop CPU with small, generated datasets and fixed seeds. The capstone brings it together: a multimodal pipeline that reads a product review's text with an LSTM and its photo with a fine-tuned CNN, and combines them to predict the review's sentiment.

modules.title: TensorFlow Foundations
modules.summary: Get to know the TensorFlow ecosystem and the tools every project uses: tensors for real data, graphs for speed and export, tf.data input pipelines, Keras preprocessing layers with the functional API, and losses and metrics that fit the task.

lessons.title: The TensorFlow ecosystem, tensors and graphs
objectives: Name the main parts of the TensorFlow ecosystem and what each is for
Work with string and ragged tensors
Explain why graphs matter for speed and deployment
key_points: TensorFlow is a platform as well as a library: Keras for building models, tf.data for input pipelines, TensorBoard for watching training, TensorFlow Serving for serving models over a network, LiteRT (formerly TensorFlow Lite) for phones and microcontrollers, and TensorFlow.js for browsers.

Tensors are multi-dimensional arrays used for data representation, and not only numbers: tf.string tensors hold text and file paths, and a RaggedTensor holds rows of different lengths, such as sentences split into words by tf.strings.split.
Every tensor has one dtype: models usually compute in float32, labels are often int32 or int64, and conversions are explicit with tf.cast.
TensorFlow graphs define the computation flow: tf.function traces Python code into a graph that TensorFlow can optimise and run without Python, which is how Keras runs its training steps.
A SavedModel stores a model's graph with its weights, so a deployed model runs in TensorFlow Serving or LiteRT without the training code or a Python interpreter.

lessons.title: Input pipelines with tf.data
objectives: Build a tf.data pipeline from arrays or a DataFrame
Order shuffle, map, batch, cache and prefetch correctly
Feed datasets to fit, evaluate and predict
key_points: tf.data.Dataset.from_tensor_slices((features, labels)) turns arrays, or a dictionary of named columns, into a dataset of single examples; fit(), evaluate() and predict() accept datasets directly, with no batch_size argument.

map(function, num_parallel_calls=tf.data.AUTOTUNE) transforms each example, such as decoding an image file; batch(32) groups examples; prefetch(tf.data.AUTOTUNE) prepares the next batch while the model trains on the current one.

shuffle(buffer_size) samples from a buffer of that many examples: a buffer as large as the dataset gives a full shuffle, a small one only local mixing. Shuffle before batching, and shuffle training data only.
cache() keeps examples in memory, or in a file, after the first pass, so reading and decoding run once; place it before random augmentation, or every epoch would see the same 'random' changes.
A dataset of dictionaries feeds a model whose keras.Input layers are named after the keys, which keeps multi-input models, such as tabular columns or text and an image, easy to wire.

lessons.title: Preprocessing layers and the functional API
objectives: Normalise numbers and encode categories with Keras preprocessing layers
Build a multi-input model with the functional API
Explain why preprocessing inside the model helps deployment
key_points: Preprocessing layers learn their state from data with adapt(): Normalization learns each feature's mean and variance, StringLookup and IntegerLookup learn a vocabulary of categories, and Discretization learns bucket boundaries.
StringLookup(output_mode="one_hot") turns a category into a one-hot vector and keeps index 0 for values it never saw ('[UNK]'), so a new category arriving in production doesn't break the model.
Adapt only on the training data: adapting on validation or test rows leaks their statistics into the model, just as fitting a scaler on all the data does.

The functional API calls layers like functions, x = layer(inputs), and builds keras.Model(inputs, outputs); it handles several named inputs, branches merged with Concatenate, shared layers and several outputs.

With preprocessing inside the model, the saved model accepts raw values (numbers and strings as they arrive) and applies exactly the transformations it was trained with, which avoids training-serving skew.

lessons.title: Losses and metrics that fit the task
objectives: Match the loss to the output layer and the labels
Choose metrics such as AUC, precision and recall
Handle class imbalance with class weights
key_points: Loss functions measure how well the model's predictions match the true labels, and training minimises the loss. It must suit the output: binary_crossentropy for one sigmoid unit, sparse_categorical_crossentropy for integer classes and softmax, mean squared or absolute error for numbers.
Huber loss behaves like squared error for small errors and like absolute error for large ones, so a few outliers in a regression target don't dominate training.

When the last layer has no activation, use the loss's from_logits=True: BinaryCrossentropy(from_logits=True) applies the sigmoid inside the loss, which is numerically safer. Passing logits to a loss that expects probabilities gives wrong values without any error.

Metrics are for people and can differ from the loss: AUC measures how well predictions rank positives above negatives at every threshold, while precision and recall depend on the threshold (0.5 by default), and accuracy misleads when one class is rare.
For imbalanced classes, fit(..., class_weight={0: 1.0, 1: 3.0}) makes mistakes on the rare class count more, or the data can be resampled; then choose the decision threshold on validation data.

print(round(float(keras.losses.BinaryCrossentropy()(y, probs)), 4),
      round(float(keras.losses.BinaryCrossentropy(from_logits=True)(y, logits)), 4))

"""Predict customer churn from a table: a tf.data pipeline, Keras preprocessing layers and the functional API."""

import os

os.environ.setdefault("TF_CPP_MIN_LOG_LEVEL", "2")

import keras
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
import tensorflow as tf
from keras import layers
from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split

NUMERIC = ["tenure_months", "monthly_charges", "support_calls"]
CATEGORICAL = ["contract", "payment"]
TARGET = "churned"


def split(df):
    train, test = train_test_split(df, test_size=0.2, random_state=0, stratify=df[TARGET])
    train, val = train_test_split(train, test_size=0.2, random_state=0, stratify=train[TARGET])
    return train, val, test


def to_features(frame):
    """A dictionary of (n, 1) arrays, one per column: what the model's named inputs expect."""
    out = {name: frame[[name]].to_numpy("float32") for name in NUMERIC}
    out.update({name: tf.constant(frame[[name]].to_numpy().astype(str)) for name in CATEGORICAL})  # string tensors
    return out


def make_dataset(frame, shuffle, batch_size=32):
    # TODO: build a tf.data pipeline from (to_features(frame), labels): from_tensor_slices, then shuffle the
    #      whole frame with seed=0 when shuffle is True, then batch(batch_size) and prefetch(tf.data.AUTOTUNE)
    return None


def build_model(train):
    inputs = {name: keras.Input(shape=(1,), name=name) for name in NUMERIC}
    inputs.update({name: keras.Input(shape=(1,), name=name, dtype="string") for name in CATEGORICAL})

    # TODO: a Normalization layer adapted on the training rows' numeric columns, applied to the concatenated
    #      numeric inputs; and a StringLookup(output_mode="one_hot") per categorical column, adapted on that
    #      column's training values
    numeric, encoded = layers.Concatenate()([inputs[name] for name in NUMERIC]), []

    x = layers.Concatenate()([numeric] + encoded)
    x = layers.Dense(32, activation="relu")(x)
    x = layers.Dropout(0.2)(x)
    output = layers.Dense(1, activation="sigmoid", name="churn_probability")(x)
    model = keras.Model(inputs, output, name="churn_model")
    model.compile(optimizer=keras.optimizers.Adam(0.001), loss="binary_crossentropy",
                  metrics=[keras.metrics.AUC(name="auc"), "accuracy"])
    return model


def main():
    keras.utils.set_random_seed(0)
    df = pd.read_csv("churn.csv")
    print(f"{len(df)} customers, churn rate {df[TARGET].mean():.3f}")
    train, val, test = split(df)
    print("train / validation / test rows:", len(train), len(val), len(test))

    train_ds = make_dataset(train, shuffle=True)
    if train_ds is None:
        print("make_dataset() isn't written yet")
        return
    features, labels = next(iter(train_ds))
    print("One batch:", {name: tuple(t.shape) for name, t in features.items()}, "labels", tuple(labels.shape))
    print("contract values in the batch:", features["contract"][:3, 0].numpy().astype(str).tolist())

    model = build_model(train)
    model.summary()
    history = model.fit(train_ds, validation_data=make_dataset(val, shuffle=False), epochs=40, verbose=0)
    best = int(np.argmax(history.history["val_auc"])) + 1
    print(f"Best validation AUC {max(history.history['val_auc']):.3f} at epoch {best}")

    loss, auc, acc = model.evaluate(make_dataset(test, shuffle=False), verbose=0)
    print(f"Test AUC {auc:.3f}, test accuracy {acc:.3f} (always guessing 'stays' scores {1 - test[TARGET].mean():.3f})")
    print("PASS: test AUC is at least 0.75" if auc >= 0.75 else "Keep going: test AUC is below 0.75")

    new = pd.DataFrame([{"tenure_months": 2, "monthly_charges": 95.0, "support_calls": 4,
                         "contract": "month-to-month", "payment": "e-wallet"},
                        {"tenure_months": 60, "monthly_charges": 45.0, "support_calls": 0,
                         "contract": "two-year", "payment": "card"}])
    print("Churn probability for two new customers:", model.predict(to_features(new), verbose=0).round(2).ravel())


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

hints: The model's keras.Input layers are named after the columns, so the dictionary keys in the dataset must match them exactly.
Normalization().adapt() takes a (rows, 3) array of the three numeric training columns; StringLookup's adapt() takes the training values of one column.
Keras wants text as string tensors; to_features() builds them with tf.constant, because Keras 3 refuses NumPy's fixed-width string arrays.

modules.title: Computer Vision Basics
modules.summary: See how convolutional networks process images: filters that detect edges and textures, padding and stride, pooling and activations, then build and train a CNN from an image folder, with data augmentation.

lessons.title: Images as tensors and the convolution operation
objectives: Describe how an image is stored as a tensor
Explain how a convolution filter produces a feature map
Work out a convolution's output size and parameter count
key_points: An image is a tensor of shape (height, width, channels), with 3 channels for colour (RGB) and 1 for greyscale, and pixel values from 0 to 255 that models usually rescale to 0-1 or −1 to 1; a batch adds a leading dimension.

Convolutions apply filters to extract features like edges and textures: a small kernel, such as 3 × 3, slides over the image and at each position takes the weighted sum of the pixels under it, producing a feature map.

The same filter weights are used at every position (weight sharing), so a Conv2D layer has (k × k × input channels + 1) × filters parameters whatever the image size, and a pattern is detected wherever it appears.

Output size: with input size n, kernel k, padding p and stride s, it's ⌊(n + 2p − k)/s⌋ + 1. padding="valid" (none) shrinks a 64-pixel side to 62 with a 3 × 3 kernel, padding="same" keeps 64 at stride 1, and a stride of 2 roughly halves it.
Stacked convolutions see ever larger regions of the input (their receptive field grows), so early layers detect edges and later layers combine them into corners, parts and objects.

lessons.title: Pooling, activations and a CNN architecture
objectives: Explain what pooling layers do
Assemble convolution blocks into an image classifier
Compare a CNN's parameter count and accuracy with an MLP's
key_points: Pooling layers reduce spatial dimensions and computational load: MaxPooling2D() keeps the largest value in each 2 × 2 window, halving height and width, has no parameters, and makes the output less sensitive to small shifts.
Activation functions introduce non-linearity into the network: a ReLU after each convolution lets stacked filters represent shapes that no single linear filter could.

A typical CNN repeats blocks of convolutions and pooling, raising the number of filters (16, 32, 64...) as the maps shrink, then ends with Flatten or GlobalAveragePooling2D and Dense layers that classify.

GlobalAveragePooling2D averages each feature map to one number, so an 8 × 8 × 64 map becomes 64 values where Flatten gives 4,096; it keeps the head small but discards where features were found, which some tasks need.
Thanks to weight sharing, a CNN usually needs far fewer parameters than an MLP on the same images and classifies them better, because it keeps the 2D structure that flattening discards.

lessons.title: Image datasets and data augmentation
objectives: Load an image folder with image_dataset_from_directory
Add augmentation layers that suit the task
Speed up an image pipeline with cache and prefetch
key_points: keras.utils.image_dataset_from_directory("shapes", image_size=(64, 64), batch_size=32) reads a folder with one subfolder per class, labels each image by its subfolder (class_names lists them alphabetically) and resizes the images.
With validation_split=0.2, call it twice, with subset="training" and subset="validation" and the same seed, so that the two subsets don't overlap.
Data augmentation helps prevent overfitting in image models: RandomFlip, RandomRotation, RandomZoom, RandomTranslation and RandomContrast layers apply random changes, only during training.
Choose augmentations that keep the label true: rotations suit shapes, cells and satellite images, while flipping a road sign or a digit can change what it means.
Call cache() and prefetch(tf.data.AUTOTUNE) on the datasets so images are decoded once and the next batch is ready while the model trains.

"""Classify circles, squares and triangles: load an image folder, then compare an MLP with a small CNN."""

import os
import subprocess
import sys

os.environ.setdefault("TF_CPP_MIN_LOG_LEVEL", "2")

import keras
import numpy as np
import tensorflow as tf
from keras import layers

IMAGE_SIZE = (64, 64)


def load():
    if not os.path.isdir("shapes"):
        subprocess.run([sys.executable, "make_shapes.py"], check=True)
    # TODO: load the shapes folder with keras.utils.image_dataset_from_directory twice, as the "training" and
    #      "validation" subsets of validation_split=0.2, with seed=0, image_size=IMAGE_SIZE and batch_size=32
    train = val = None
    return train, val


def mlp():
    return keras.Sequential([
        keras.Input(shape=IMAGE_SIZE + (3,)),
        layers.Rescaling(1.0 / 255),
        layers.Flatten(),
        layers.Dense(64, activation="relu"),
        layers.Dense(3, activation="softmax"),
    ], name="mlp")


def cnn(augment=False):
    model = keras.Sequential([keras.Input(shape=IMAGE_SIZE + (3,))], name="cnn_augmented" if augment else "cnn")
    if augment:
        model.add(layers.RandomFlip("horizontal_and_vertical"))
        model.add(layers.RandomRotation(0.25))
    model.add(layers.Rescaling(1.0 / 255))
    # TODO: three blocks, each two Conv2D(filters, 3, padding="same", activation="relu") layers and a
    #      MaxPooling2D(), with 16, 32 and 64 filters; then Flatten, Dropout(0.3), Dense(64, activation="relu")
    #      and a Dense(3, activation="softmax") output
    model.add(layers.Flatten()); model.add(layers.Dense(3, activation="softmax"))
    return model


def train_and_score(model, train, val, epochs=20):
    keras.utils.set_random_seed(0)
    model.compile(optimizer="adam", loss="sparse_categorical_crossentropy", metrics=["accuracy"])
    h = model.fit(train, validation_data=val, epochs=epochs, verbose=0).history
    print(f"{model.name:14} parameters {model.count_params():7,}  best val_accuracy {max(h['val_accuracy']):.3f}  "
          f"last {h['val_accuracy'][-1]:.3f}")


def main():
    keras.utils.set_random_seed(0)
    train, val = load()
    if train is None:
        print("load() isn't written yet")
        return
    print("Classes:", train.class_names)
    images, labels = next(iter(train))
    print("A batch:", images.shape, images.dtype.name, "pixel range", float(tf.reduce_min(images)), "to",
          float(tf.reduce_max(images)), "labels", labels[:8].numpy())
    train, val = train.cache().prefetch(tf.data.AUTOTUNE), val.cache().prefetch(tf.data.AUTOTUNE)
    model = cnn()
    model.summary()
    for model in (mlp(), cnn(), cnn(augment=True)):
        train_and_score(model, train, val)


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

modules.summary: Reuse what large pre-trained networks have learned: transfer learning with a frozen base, fine-tuning its top layers, and the ideas behind object detection and image segmentation, from bounding boxes and IoU to classifying every pixel.

lessons.title: Transfer learning with pre-trained models
objectives: Explain why features learned on ImageNet transfer to new tasks
Build a model from a frozen pre-trained base and a new head
Prepare inputs the way the base expects
key_points: Transfer learning utilises pre-trained models, such as ResNet50, MobileNetV2 or EfficientNet trained on ImageNet's 1.2 million labelled photos, for new tasks: their early layers detect edges, textures and shapes that are useful almost everywhere.

keras.applications.MobileNetV2(include_top=False, weights="imagenet", input_shape=(96, 96, 3)) gives the convolutional base without its 1,000-class classifier; the weights download once into ~/.keras/models.

Freeze the base (base.trainable = False), add a new head, such as GlobalAveragePooling2D, Dropout and a Dense softmax over the new classes, and train only the head; with little data this beats training from scratch by a wide margin.

Each pre-trained model expects its inputs prepared its own way, given by its preprocess_input function: MobileNetV2 scales pixels from 0-255 to −1 to 1, while ResNet50 subtracts ImageNet's mean colour from BGR-ordered channels.
Call the base with training=False, base(x, training=False), so its batch normalisation layers keep their ImageNet statistics, even after the base is unfrozen for fine-tuning.

lessons.title: Fine-tuning
objectives: Fine-tune the top layers of a pre-trained base
Choose the learning rate and the layers to unfreeze
Recognise when fine-tuning overfits
key_points: Fine-tuning adjusts the weights of a pre-trained model for specific data: once the new head has trained, unfreeze the top layers of the base, whose features are the most specific to ImageNet, and keep training.
Train the head first: a randomly initialised head sends large, noisy gradients into the base and can wreck its pre-trained features.
Fine-tune with a much lower learning rate, often 10 to 100 times lower (such as 1e-5 with Adam), and recompile after changing trainable, because compile() fixes which weights the optimiser updates.
Unfreeze only as much as the data supports: the top 20 to 30 layers of MobileNetV2 for a few hundred images, more of the network when there's far more data.
Watch the validation curve: falling validation accuracy while training accuracy rises means the model is overfitting the small dataset, so unfreeze fewer layers, augment more or stop earlier.

lessons.title: Object detection and image segmentation
objectives: Describe what object detection outputs and how it's evaluated
Compute intersection over union and apply non-maximum suppression
Distinguish semantic, instance and panoptic segmentation
key_points: Object detection identifies and locates multiple objects within an image: for each object it outputs a bounding box, such as [x1, y1, x2, y2], a class and a confidence score.

Intersection over union (IoU), the overlap of two boxes divided by the area they cover together, measures how well boxes match: 1 for identical, 0 for disjoint. A detection often counts as correct at IoU 0.5 or more, and mean average precision (mAP) summarises precision and recall over classes.

Detectors propose many overlapping boxes per object; non-maximum suppression keeps the highest-scoring box, drops every box overlapping it by more than an IoU threshold, and repeats down the list (tf.image.non_max_suppression does this).

Two-stage detectors such as Faster R-CNN propose regions first and then classify them; one-stage detectors such as YOLO, SSD and RetinaNet predict boxes and classes in one pass and are usually faster.

Image segmentation classifies each pixel in an image: semantic segmentation labels every pixel with a class, instance segmentation also separates individual objects (as Mask R-CNN does), and panoptic segmentation combines the two.

Segmentation networks such as U-Net shrink the image into features with an encoder and upsample back to full size with a decoder, with skip connections carrying fine detail across; they train with per-pixel cross-entropy and are judged by IoU or the Dice score.

"""Transfer learning with MobileNetV2 on a small image set: train from scratch, extract features, then fine-tune."""

import os
import subprocess
import sys

os.environ.setdefault("TF_CPP_MIN_LOG_LEVEL", "2")

import keras
import tensorflow as tf
from keras import layers

SIZE = (96, 96)


def load():
    if not os.path.isdir("shapes96"):
        subprocess.run([sys.executable, "make_shapes.py", "--size", "96", "--per-class", "40", "--colours", "random",
                        "--out", "shapes96", "--seed", "1"], check=True)
    kw = dict(validation_split=0.25, seed=0, image_size=SIZE, batch_size=16)
    train = keras.utils.image_dataset_from_directory("shapes96", subset="training", **kw)
    val = keras.utils.image_dataset_from_directory("shapes96", subset="validation", **kw)
    return train.cache().prefetch(tf.data.AUTOTUNE), val.cache().prefetch(tf.data.AUTOTUNE)


def small_cnn():
    model = keras.Sequential([keras.Input(shape=SIZE + (3,)), layers.Rescaling(1.0 / 255)], name="from_scratch")
    for filters in (16, 32, 64):
        model.add(layers.Conv2D(filters, 3, padding="same", activation="relu"))
        model.add(layers.MaxPooling2D())
    model.add(layers.GlobalAveragePooling2D())
    model.add(layers.Dense(3, activation="softmax"))
    return model


def transfer_model():
    """MobileNetV2 trained on ImageNet, without its classifier, frozen, with a new head for three classes."""
    # TODO: create keras.applications.MobileNetV2(input_shape=SIZE + (3,), include_top=False, weights="imagenet")
    #      and freeze it (base.trainable = False)
    base = None
    inputs = keras.Input(shape=SIZE + (3,))
    x = layers.Rescaling(1.0 / 127.5, offset=-1)(inputs)  # what mobilenet_v2.preprocess_input does: 0-255 to -1..1
    # TODO: call the base with training=False (keeps its batch normalisation in inference mode), then add
    #      GlobalAveragePooling2D, Dropout(0.2) and a Dense(3, activation="softmax") head
    outputs = layers.Dense(3, activation="softmax")(layers.Flatten()(x))
    return keras.Model(inputs, outputs, name="mobilenet_transfer"), base


def fit(model, train, val, epochs, lr, label=None):
    model.compile(optimizer=keras.optimizers.Adam(lr), loss="sparse_categorical_crossentropy", metrics=["accuracy"])
    h = model.fit(train, validation_data=val, epochs=epochs, verbose=0).history
    trainable = sum(int(tf.size(w)) for w in model.trainable_weights)
    print(f"{label or model.name:20} lr={lr:<7} trainable parameters {trainable:9,}  val_accuracy {h['val_accuracy'][-1]:.3f} "
          f"(best {max(h['val_accuracy']):.3f})")


def main():
    keras.utils.set_random_seed(0)
    train, val = load()
    fit(small_cnn(), train, val, epochs=20, lr=1e-3)

    keras.utils.set_random_seed(0)
    model, base = transfer_model()
    if base is None:
        print("transfer_model() isn't written yet")
        return
    print(f"MobileNetV2 base: {len(base.layers)} layers, output shape {base.output.shape}")
    fit(model, train, val, epochs=10, lr=1e-3)

    # TODO: fine-tune: unfreeze the base, then freeze all but its last 30 layers; recompile (fit() does it here)
    #      with a learning rate of 1e-5 and train 10 more epochs


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

lessons.title: Standardising and tokenising text
objectives: Explain standardisation, tokenisation and vocabularies
Turn text into padded sequences of token ids with TextVectorization
Handle words the vocabulary doesn't contain
key_points: Tokenisation converts text into numerical sequences: standardise the text (lower case, strip punctuation), split it into tokens (words, subwords or characters), and map each token to an integer id from a vocabulary built on the training data.

keras.layers.TextVectorization(max_tokens=2000, output_sequence_length=30) does all three; adapt(texts) keeps the most frequent tokens, and in its int mode id 0 is padding and id 1 is '[UNK]', the out-of-vocabulary token.
output_sequence_length pads short texts with 0s and cuts long ones, so every example has the same length and examples can be batched.

Every token missing from the vocabulary becomes [UNK], so max_tokens trades coverage against model size; the subword tokenisers of transformer models (WordPiece, byte-pair encoding) split rare words into known pieces instead.
Keeping the vectoriser inside the model means the deployed model accepts raw strings and tokenises them exactly as in training.

lessons.title: Stop words, stemming and lemmatisation
objectives: Decide when to remove stop words
Distinguish stemming from lemmatisation
key_points: Stop words are common words often removed during preprocessing, such as 'the', 'is' and 'and', to shrink a bag-of-words vocabulary; scikit-learn's ENGLISH_STOP_WORDS list holds 318 of them.
Removing them can destroy meaning: scikit-learn's list includes 'not', 'no' and 'never', so 'not good' becomes 'good'. Sentiment models and most neural models keep stop words.

Stemming cuts words down to a root by rule: NLTK's Porter stemmer turns 'connected' and 'connecting' into 'connect', but 'studies' into 'studi'. Lemmatisation looks up the dictionary form instead, so 'studies' becomes 'study'.
Both shrink the vocabulary, which can help bag-of-words models on small datasets; embedding models and transformer tokenisers generally work on the original words or subwords.

lessons.title: Bag-of-words, n-grams and TF-IDF
objectives: Represent documents as bags of words and n-grams
Explain how TF-IDF weighs words
Build a TF-IDF text classifier in Keras
key_points: Bag-of-words represents text based on word frequency: each document becomes a vector with one position per vocabulary word, holding 1 or 0 (multi_hot) or the word's count (count); word order is lost.
n-grams add short word sequences as features: with ngrams=2, TextVectorization adds bigrams such as 'not good', which recovers some of the order that matters, at the cost of a bigger vocabulary.

TF-IDF weighs words based on their importance in a document: term frequency times inverse document frequency, so words in almost every document (like 'it') get low weights and rarer, telling words high ones.

Keras's TextVectorization(output_mode="tf_idf") learns IDF weights in adapt() as log(1 + N/(1 + df)), for N documents of which df contain the term; scikit-learn's TfidfVectorizer uses ln((1 + N)/(1 + df)) + 1 and normalises each row, so the numbers differ but the idea is the same.
A linear or small dense model on TF-IDF or n-gram features is a fast, strong baseline for text classification, and the score a sequence model has to beat.

os.environ.setdefault("TF_CPP_MIN_LOG_LEVEL", "2")

import keras
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
import tensorflow as tf
from keras import layers
from sklearn.feature_extraction.text import ENGLISH_STOP_WORDS, TfidfVectorizer
from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression
from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split


def load():
    df = pd.concat([pd.read_csv("reviews_1.csv"), pd.read_csv("reviews_2.csv")], ignore_index=True)
    train, test = train_test_split(df, test_size=0.25, random_state=0, stratify=df["label"])
    return train, test


def remove_stop_words(texts):
    return [" ".join(w for w in t.lower().replace(".", " ").replace(",", " ").split() if w not in ENGLISH_STOP_WORDS)
            for t in texts]


def bag_of_words_model(train_texts, mode, ngrams=None):
    # TODO: a TextVectorization layer with max_tokens=2000, the given output_mode and ngrams, adapted on the
    #      training texts; then a model: string Input of shape (1,) -> vectorizer -> Dense(16, relu) -> Dropout(0.3)
    #      -> Dense(1, sigmoid); return the model and the vectorizer
    return None, None


def score(name, train_texts, y_train, test_texts, y_test, mode, ngrams=None):
    keras.utils.set_random_seed(0)
    model, vectorizer = bag_of_words_model(train_texts, mode, ngrams)
    if model is None:
        print("bag_of_words_model() isn't written yet")
        return None
    model.compile(optimizer="adam", loss="binary_crossentropy", metrics=["accuracy"])
    as_strings = lambda texts: tf.constant([[t] for t in texts])  # Keras takes string tensors, not NumPy str arrays
    model.fit(as_strings(train_texts), y_train, epochs=20, batch_size=32, verbose=0)
    acc = model.evaluate(as_strings(test_texts), y_test, verbose=0)[1]
    print(f"{name:30} vocabulary {vectorizer.vocabulary_size():5}  test accuracy {acc:.3f}")
    return vectorizer


def main():
    train, test = load()
    X_train, y_train = train["text"].tolist(), train["label"].to_numpy()
    X_test, y_test = test["text"].tolist(), test["label"].to_numpy()
    print(f"{len(train)} training and {len(test)} test reviews; share positive: {y_train.mean():.3f}")
    print("Example:", X_train[0])

    tokens = layers.TextVectorization(max_tokens=2000, output_mode="int", output_sequence_length=12)
    tokens.adapt(X_train)
    print("First vocabulary entries:", tokens.get_vocabulary()[:8])
    print("As token ids:", tokens([X_train[0]]).numpy()[0].tolist())
    print("'not' is an English stop word in scikit-learn's list:", "not" in ENGLISH_STOP_WORDS)
    print("Without stop words:", remove_stop_words([X_train[0]])[0])

    multi = score("multi-hot words", X_train, y_train, X_test, y_test, "multi_hot")
    if multi is None:
        return
    score("word counts", X_train, y_train, X_test, y_test, "count")
    tfidf = score("TF-IDF words and bigrams", X_train, y_train, X_test, y_test, "tf_idf", ngrams=2)
    score("multi-hot, stop words removed", remove_stop_words(X_train), y_train, remove_stop_words(X_test), y_test, "multi_hot")

    vocab = tfidf.get_vocabulary()
    for word in ("it", "flimsy", "not flimsy"):
        if word in vocab:  # a text containing the term once: its TF-IDF value is the term's IDF weight
            print(f"IDF of {word!r}: {tfidf([word]).numpy()[0][vocab.index(word)]:.3f}")

    sk = TfidfVectorizer(ngram_range=(1, 2))
    baseline = LogisticRegression(max_iter=1000).fit(sk.fit_transform(X_train), y_train)
    print(f"{'scikit-learn TF-IDF + logistic':30} vocabulary {len(sk.vocabulary_):5}  test accuracy "
          f"{baseline.score(sk.transform(X_test), y_test):.3f}")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

modules.title: Embeddings and RNNs
modules.summary: Represent words as learned dense vectors, process sequences with recurrent layers (SimpleRNN, GRU and LSTM), see how encoder-decoder models handle tasks like translation, and finish by saving, exporting and serving a text model.

lessons.title: Word embeddings
objectives: Explain how embeddings represent words as dense vectors
Use an Embedding layer with masking
Compare learned, pre-trained and contextual embeddings
key_points: Embeddings represent words as dense vectors in a continuous space: Embedding(input_dim=vocabulary size, output_dim=32) is a trainable lookup table with one row of 32 numbers per token id.
Training moves words used in similar ways close together, so the cosine similarity of two vectors (1 for the same direction, −1 for opposite) reflects how similar the words are for the task learned.
mask_zero=True tells later layers to skip padding (id 0), so a recurrent layer doesn't read padding as words; it relies on the vocabulary reserving 0 for padding, as TextVectorization does.

Pre-trained embeddings such as word2vec, GloVe and fastText, learned from billions of words, can start the layer off when labelled data is scarce; fastText also builds vectors for unseen words from character n-grams.
These are static embeddings, one vector per word in every context; transformer models produce contextual embeddings, in which 'bank' gets different vectors in 'river bank' and 'bank account'.

lessons.title: Recurrent networks: SimpleRNN, LSTM and GRU
objectives: Explain how an RNN processes a sequence with a hidden state
Explain how LSTM and GRU gates mitigate vanishing gradients
Count a recurrent layer's parameters and use Bidirectional
key_points: RNNs process sequential data by maintaining a hidden state: at each step h_t = tanh(W x_t + U h_(t−1) + b), with the same weights at every step, so the last state summarises the whole sequence.

Training unrolls the network over the steps and backpropagates through them, multiplying by the same weights again and again, so gradients tend to vanish (or explode) over long sequences and a SimpleRNN forgets what came many steps before.

LSTMs mitigate the vanishing gradient problem in standard RNNs: a cell state carries information forward through additive updates, controlled by forget, input and output gates. GRUs merge this into update and reset gates, with fewer parameters.

With u units and d input features, SimpleRNN has u(u + d + 1) parameters and LSTM four times as many, 4u(u + d + 1); Keras's GRU has 3u(u + d + 2), because its default reset_after=True adds a second bias.
Bidirectional(LSTM(32)) runs one LSTM forwards and one backwards and joins their outputs (64 values); return_sequences=True returns every step's output, which a second, stacked recurrent layer needs.

steps.do: Build each recurrent layer with 32 units on sequences of 30 steps with 16 features, and count its parameters.
steps.code:
import keras
from keras import layers
for layer in (layers.SimpleRNN(32), layers.LSTM(32), layers.GRU(32), layers.Bidirectional(layers.LSTM(32))):
    model = keras.Sequential([keras.Input((30, 16)), layer])
    print(type(layer).__name__, model.count_params(), model.output_shape)
steps.see: SimpleRNN 1568 (None, 32) | LSTM 6272 (None, 32) | GRU 4800 (None, 32) | Bidirectional 12544 (None, 64). 32 x (32 + 16 + 1) = 1,568 for SimpleRNN, 4 times that for LSTM, 3 x 32 x (32 + 16 + 2) for GRU.

steps.do: Ask for every step's output, as a second recurrent layer stacked on top would need.

lessons.title: Sequence-to-sequence models and attention
objectives: Describe the encoder-decoder architecture
Explain why attention, and then transformers, replaced plain RNN encoders
key_points: Sequence-to-sequence models are used for tasks like translation and summarisation: an encoder reads the input sequence into a representation, and a decoder generates the output one token at a time.

In training the decoder is usually fed the correct previous token rather than its own guess (teacher forcing), which speeds learning; at inference it feeds back its own outputs, often with beam search.

A plain RNN encoder squeezes the whole input into one fixed-size state, a bottleneck for long inputs; attention (Bahdanau et al., 2014) lets the decoder look back at every encoder state and weight the relevant ones at each step.

Transformers (Vaswani et al., 2017) drop recurrence and use attention alone, which trains in parallel over long sequences; they now dominate translation and language modelling, while RNNs remain useful for small, streaming or on-device sequence tasks.

lessons.title: Saving, exporting and serving models
objectives: Save and reload a Keras model in the .keras format
Export a SavedModel and call its serving function
Serve a model with TensorFlow Serving's REST API
key_points: model.save("sentiment.keras") writes the architecture, the weights, the compile settings and the state of preprocessing layers (such as a TextVectorization vocabulary) to one file; keras.models.load_model brings it back in Python for more training or prediction.
model.export("sentiment_savedmodel") writes a TensorFlow SavedModel, a graph plus weights, with a serve endpoint: tf.saved_model.load(path).serve(inputs) runs it without the model's Python code.

TensorFlow Serving loads SavedModels from numbered version folders (models/sentiment/1) and answers REST requests on port 8501, such as POST /v1/models/sentiment:predict with {"instances": [...]}; the official tensorflow/serving Docker image is the usual way to run it.
With preprocessing inside the exported model, clients send raw text or values, and the server applies exactly the transformations used in training.

"""Sentiment with embeddings and recurrent layers, then save, reload and export the model for serving."""

import os

os.environ.setdefault("TF_CPP_MIN_LOG_LEVEL", "2")

import keras
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
import tensorflow as tf
from keras import layers
from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split

MAX_TOKENS, SEQ_LEN, EMBED = 2000, 30, 32
PROBES = ["Really great.", "Not great at all.", "It is flimsy.", "Not flimsy at all."]


def load():
    df = pd.concat([pd.read_csv("reviews_1.csv"), pd.read_csv("reviews_2.csv")], ignore_index=True)
    train, test = train_test_split(df, test_size=0.25, random_state=0, stratify=df["label"])
    as_strings = lambda frame: tf.constant([[t] for t in frame["text"]])  # (n, 1) string tensors
    return as_strings(train), train["label"].to_numpy("float32"), as_strings(test), test["label"].to_numpy("float32")


def sequence_model(vectorizer, kind):
    inputs = keras.Input(shape=(1,), dtype="string", name="text")
    x = vectorizer(inputs)  # (batch, SEQ_LEN) token ids, 0 for padding
    # TODO: an Embedding(MAX_TOKENS, EMBED, mask_zero=True) so that padding is ignored, then the recurrent layer:
    #      SimpleRNN(32), GRU(32), LSTM(32) or Bidirectional(LSTM(32)) depending on kind
    x = layers.GlobalAveragePooling1D()(layers.Embedding(MAX_TOKENS, EMBED)(x))
    x = layers.Dropout(0.3)(x)
    outputs = layers.Dense(1, activation="sigmoid", name="positive")(x)
    return keras.Model(inputs, outputs, name=kind)


def main():
    keras.utils.set_random_seed(0)
    X_train, y_train, X_test, y_test = load()
    vectorizer = layers.TextVectorization(max_tokens=MAX_TOKENS, output_sequence_length=SEQ_LEN, name="vectorizer")
    vectorizer.adapt(X_train[:, 0])
    print("Padded token ids:", vectorizer(["Not great at all."]).numpy()[0][:8].tolist())

    best = None
    for kind in ("simple_rnn", "gru", "lstm", "bidirectional_lstm"):
        keras.utils.set_random_seed(0)
        model = sequence_model(vectorizer, kind)
        rnn_params = model.layers[3].count_params()
        model.compile(optimizer="adam", loss="binary_crossentropy", metrics=["accuracy"])
        model.fit(X_train, y_train, epochs=12, batch_size=32, validation_split=0.15, verbose=0)
        acc = model.evaluate(X_test, y_test, verbose=0)[1]
        print(f"{kind:20} recurrent parameters {rnn_params:6,}  test accuracy {acc:.3f}")
        if best is None or acc > best[1]:
            best = (model, acc)

    model = best[0]
    print(f"Best: {model.name}. Probabilities for the probes:")
    for text, p in zip(PROBES, model.predict(tf.constant([[p] for p in PROBES]), verbose=0).ravel()):
        print(f"  {text:22} {p:.2f}")

    embedding = model.get_layer("embedding").get_weights()[0]
    vocab = vectorizer.get_vocabulary()
    def similarity(a, b):
        u, v = embedding[vocab.index(a)], embedding[vocab.index(b)]
        return float(u @ v / (np.linalg.norm(u) * np.linalg.norm(v)))
    print(f"Cosine similarity: great/excellent {similarity('great', 'excellent'):.2f}, "
          f"great/terrible {similarity('great', 'terrible'):.2f}")

    # TODO: save the model as sentiment.keras, load it back with keras.models.load_model and check that it gives
    #      the same predictions; then export a SavedModel with model.export("sentiment_savedmodel"), load it with
    #      tf.saved_model.load and call its serve() function on a batch of raw strings


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

project.title: Multimodal sentiment analysis pipeline
project.brief: Online shops collect reviews that pair a few words with a photo of the product as it arrived. Build a TensorFlow pipeline that predicts each review's sentiment from both. make_multimodal.py generates the dataset: 900 reviews, each a short text and a 96 x 96 photo, labelled positive or negative. In about a third of the reviews the text doesn't reveal the sentiment, in about a third the photo shows only the closed parcel, and a few labels are wrong; two columns record which reviews are which, for analysis only. multimodal_starter.py loads the data into tf.data pipelines with a text input and a photo input, split into training, validation and test sets. Train an LSTM or GRU text model, fine-tune a pre-trained CNN such as MobileNetV2 on the photos (head first, then the top layers at a low learning rate), and combine the two, either by averaging their probabilities or with one functional model that concatenates both branches before its output. """Generate the capstone's multimodal dataset: product reviews, each with a photo of the product as it arrived.

    python make_multimodal.py            # writes multimodal/reviews.csv and multimodal/photos/*.png

Each review is positive (1) or negative (0). In about 30% of reviews the text doesn't say which (it only talks
about delivery or colour), and in about 30% the photo doesn't show it (only the closed box is pictured), so a
model that uses both can do better than either alone. A few labels are wrong, as in real data. The columns
text_informative and photo_informative record which reviews are which: use them to analyse results, never as
model inputs.
"""

import csv
import math
import random
from pathlib import Path

import numpy as np
from PIL import Image, ImageDraw

N, SIZE, SEED = 900, 96, 2026
OUT = Path("multimodal")

POSITIVE = ["great", "excellent", "works perfectly", "sturdy", "well made", "good value", "easy to use",
            "really happy with it", "brilliant", "love it"]
NEGATIVE = ["terrible", "arrived broken", "poor quality", "waste of money", "stopped working", "flimsy",
            "cracked", "disappointing", "hard to use", "returned it"]
NEUTRAL = ["Delivery took four days.", "The colour matches the photos.", "It came in a cardboard box.",
           "Ordered it on Monday.", "The instructions are short.", "Bought it for my sister."]
PRODUCTS = ["mug", "bowl", "vase", "teapot", "plate", "jar"]


def text_for(rng, label, clear):
    product = rng.choice(PRODUCTS)
    parts = [rng.choice(["My new {p}.", "Bought this {p}.", "The {p} I ordered.", "A {p} for the kitchen."]).format(p=product)]
    if clear:
        phrases = POSITIVE if label else NEGATIVE
        for phrase in rng.sample(phrases, rng.choice([1, 2])):
            parts.append(rng.choice(["It is {w}.", "{W}.", "Honestly {w}."]).format(w=phrase, W=phrase.capitalize()))
    parts += rng.sample(NEUTRAL, rng.choice([1, 2]))
    return " ".join(parts)


def photo_for(rng, label, clear):
    """A product on a table: whole if positive, cracked and chipped if negative; or just the closed box."""
    img = Image.new("RGB", (SIZE, SIZE), tuple(int(v) for v in rng.integers(170, 236, 3)))
    d = ImageDraw.Draw(img)
    if not clear:  # only the parcel is shown
        x0, y0 = rng.integers(10, 30, 2)
        d.rectangle([x0, y0, x0 + 55, y0 + 50], fill=(160, 120, 70))
        d.rectangle([x0 + 24, y0, x0 + 31, y0 + 50], fill=(210, 190, 140))
    else:
        colour = tuple(int(v) for v in rng.integers(20, 150, 3))
        cx, cy, r = SIZE / 2 + rng.uniform(-10, 10), SIZE / 2 + rng.uniform(-8, 8), rng.uniform(22, 30)
        d.ellipse([cx - r, cy - r, cx + r, cy + r], fill=colour)
        if not label:
            for _ in range(int(rng.integers(2, 5))):  # dark cracks across the product
                x, y = cx + rng.uniform(-r / 2, r / 2), cy + rng.uniform(-r / 2, r / 2)
                points = [(x, y)]
                for _ in range(4):
                    a = rng.uniform(0, 2 * math.pi)
                    x, y = x + 7 * math.cos(a), y + 7 * math.sin(a)
                    points.append((x, y))
                d.line(points, fill=(15, 15, 15), width=2)
            a = rng.uniform(0, 2 * math.pi)  # a chip out of the rim
            px, py = cx + r * math.cos(a), cy + r * math.sin(a)
            d.ellipse([px - 7, py - 7, px + 7, py + 7], fill=img.getpixel((2, 2)))
    pixels = np.asarray(img, dtype=np.int16) + rng.integers(-20, 21, (SIZE, SIZE, 3))
    return Image.fromarray(np.clip(pixels, 0, 255).astype(np.uint8))


def main():
    text_rng, image_rng = random.Random(SEED), np.random.default_rng(SEED)
    (OUT / "photos").mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
    rows = []
    for i in range(N):
        label = int(text_rng.random() < 0.5)
        text_clear, photo_clear = text_rng.random() >= 0.3, text_rng.random() >= 0.3
        name = f"photo_{i:04d}.png"
        photo_for(image_rng, label, photo_clear).save(OUT / "photos" / name)
        noisy = text_rng.random() < 0.03
        rows.append([i, text_for(text_rng, label, text_clear), name, 1 - label if noisy else label,
                     int(text_clear), int(photo_clear)])
    with open(OUT / "reviews.csv", "w", newline="") as f:
        w = csv.writer(f)
        w.writerow(["review_id", "text", "photo", "label", "text_informative", "photo_informative"])
        w.writerows(rows)
    print(f"Wrote {N} reviews and photos to {OUT}/")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

"""Capstone starter: the multimodal reviews as tf.data pipelines with two inputs, "text" and "photo".

Run python make_multimodal.py first. Then build, train and compare a text model, a photo model and a fused model.
"""

import os

os.environ.setdefault("TF_CPP_MIN_LOG_LEVEL", "2")

import keras
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
import tensorflow as tf
from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split

DATA = "multimodal"
SIZE = (96, 96)


def load_split():
    df = pd.read_csv(f"{DATA}/reviews.csv")
    train, test = train_test_split(df, test_size=0.2, random_state=0, stratify=df["label"])
    train, val = train_test_split(train, test_size=0.2, random_state=0, stratify=train["label"])
    return train, val, test


def load_photo(path):
    image = tf.io.decode_png(tf.io.read_file(path), channels=3)
    return tf.image.resize(image, SIZE)  # float32 pixels, 0 to 255


def make_dataset(frame, shuffle, batch_size=32):
    """Batches of ({"text": (batch, 1) strings, "photo": (batch, 96, 96, 3) pixels}, (batch,) labels)."""
    paths = [f"{DATA}/photos/{name}" for name in frame["photo"]]
    ds = tf.data.Dataset.from_tensor_slices(({"text": frame["text"].tolist(), "photo": paths},
                                             frame["label"].to_numpy("float32")))
    if shuffle:
        ds = ds.shuffle(len(frame), seed=0)
    ds = ds.map(lambda x, y: ({"text": tf.expand_dims(x["text"], -1), "photo": load_photo(x["photo"])}, y),
                num_parallel_calls=tf.data.AUTOTUNE)
    return ds.batch(batch_size).prefetch(tf.data.AUTOTUNE)


def main():
    keras.utils.set_random_seed(0)
    train, val, test = load_split()
    print("train / validation / test reviews:", len(train), len(val), len(test))
    print("share positive in training:", round(float(train["label"].mean()), 3))
    features, labels = next(iter(make_dataset(train, shuffle=True)))
    print("A batch:", {k: tuple(v.shape) for k, v in features.items()}, "labels", tuple(labels.shape))
    # Your work: a text model (TextVectorization, Embedding, LSTM), a photo model (MobileNetV2, frozen, then
    # fine-tuned) and a fused model with both inputs; compare all three on the validation data, then test once.


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()
